planting.note: Set rhizomes shallowly, just below the soil surface, after the soil has warmed in spring; this species resents cold, wet soil while dormant.

directions: Native to the forest floor of Myanmar and Thailand, this dwarf ginger forms a tight rosette of rounded, near-black leaves overlaid with a silvery sheen, among the most dramatically colored foliage in the genus. Grow it in bright, indirect light in humus-rich, fast-draining soil, watering freely through the warm growing season but withholding water almost entirely once the foliage collapses into winter dormancy. Inch-wide lavender flowers with a white throat open in a slow, continuous succession through summer, each lasting only a single day. Because it stays so low and compact, it is best used as a container specimen or intimate groundcover in a shaded, frost-free bed rather than a mass planting.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide and replant dormant rhizomes in spring once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60F.

directions: Unlike most peacock gingers, which hug the ground, this Laotian species builds an upright clump of lance-shaped leaves striped with metallic silver bands down the midrib, giving it a bolder, more architectural presence in a shade border. It thrives in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade and needs protection wherever frost threatens, since it dies back hard in winter and resprouts from the rhizome the following spring. Small pale flowers appear intermittently among the foliage but are secondary to the striped leaves that give the plant its appeal. Use it as a textural accent behind lower-growing Kaempferia and Globba species in a layered tropical shade planting.

planting.note: Plant shallow rhizome divisions in spring; this cultivar is more cold-tolerant than most peacock gingers and can be left in the ground in mild-winter zone 8 gardens with heavy mulch.

directions: This selection of the Southeast Asian peacock ginger lays its oval leaves nearly flat against the soil, each one overlaid with an intricate checkerboard pattern of burgundy and bronze that gives the cultivar its name. It is one of the more vigorous and cold-hardy peacock gingers in cultivation, tolerating a touch more direct morning sun than its relatives without scorching as long as the soil stays consistently moist. Small lavender flowers appear sporadically above the foliage in summer, but the patterned leaves are the main event. Use it as a striking low groundcover at the front of a shaded bed or along a woodland path edge where its foliage pattern can be appreciated up close.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or collected bulbils in spring in humus-rich soil; established clumps also self-propagate readily from bulbils that form along the flowering stems.

directions: Native to Southeast Asian forest understories, this dancing-ladies ginger is distinguished from its relatives by rounded, globe-shaped flower bracts rather than the elongated spikes typical of the genus, with clusters of rich purple bracts releasing small dangling yellow 'dancer' flowers through summer. It is one of the easiest and most reliable Globba species for shaded southern gardens, tolerating dappled shade to fairly deep shade as long as moisture stays consistent. Unlike many gingers that spread only by rhizome division, it also produces bulbils along the inflorescence that drop and root readily, forming naturalized colonies over a few seasons. Where winters bring hard frost, lift and store the rhizomes dry indoors, or grow the plant in a container that can be moved under cover.

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions 1-2 inches deep in spring once soil has warmed; new shoots emerge slowly and benefit from consistent warmth and moisture.

directions: This white-bracted selection of the Thai and Vietnamese dancing-ladies ginger produces pendant clusters of pure white bracts from which small bright yellow flowers dangle and flutter, a striking contrast to the pink- and purple-bracted forms more commonly grown. Plants form an upright clump of cane-like stems clothed in broad tropical leaves, dying back to the rhizome each winter and re-emerging reliably in late spring once soil has warmed. Grow it in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where the pale bracts show up especially well against darker foliage companions. Individual flowering clusters can persist for a month or more, making it one of the longer-blooming ornamental gingers for a shaded border or large container.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist soil; this patented selection flowers most heavily on second-year clumps.

directions: Bred and patented as a richly colored improvement on the species, this dancing-ladies ginger carries deep pink to ruby bracts with contrasting cranberry bracteoles and a purplish cast to the new foliage, making it noticeably darker and more saturated than typical Globba winitii. It flowers more profusely and over a longer season than the wild form, sending up pendant clusters from the leaf axils through summer and into fall wherever nights stay warm. Grow it as its Thai and Vietnamese parent species prefers, in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial to full shade, and let it die back to the rhizome after the first hard frost. It combines well with variegated shade foliage plants that pick up the ruby tones in its bracts and new leaves.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
